extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and playwrights studying dramatic theory and Aristotle's Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating classical tragedy according to Aristotle: criteria for plot, character, diction, music, presentation, unity, magnitude, believability, and the relative roles of the elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six factors of a Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A Tragedy must have six Factors, analytically speaking: Story, Psychology (Character), Diction (Language), Intelligence, Presentation, Music. "Two Factors go to the Clothing, one to the Treatment, three to the Theme."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each factor plays a distinct role: Story/psychology/intelligence belong primarily to theme and substance; diction and music to clothing; presentation to exhibition. These are to be considered as parts of the whole dramatic art rather than interchangeable extras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Story (Plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Story (group of occurrences) is the heart and soul of Tragedy and the most important factor; the events (Story) constitute the ultimate factor in a Tragedy, to which the others must be subordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong plot portraying a complete 'chapter of life' will succeed better than exquisite psychology alone. The chief fascinations of Tragedy (e.g. Irony of Fate, Disclosure of Mistaken Identity) are parts of the Story. Beginners master diction and psychology sooner than plot-construction, showing plot's central difficulty and importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character/Psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatis personae must be beings of 'character and intellect' because fictitious conduct derives its qualities from those two; character is exhibited in both speech and action while intellect is confined to what is displayed in words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters determine variation in story, diction, music, and presentation. Psychology functions as 'an index to the quality of the purpose' especially where ulterior motives are obscure; speakers should be natural (untrained rhetoric) unless their role requires rhetorical training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence (Speech of Reasoning/Proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence is the faculty of telling 'what is within and suits a case' and applies to passages where characters prove, disprove, or generalize—i.e., the verbal demonstration or reasoning performed on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intelligence where utterances involve demonstration or where the speaker has a purpose to clarify; avoid employing 'intelligence' passages where there is no purpose or where psychology suffices (e.g., demonstrations of natural law do not admit psychology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction (language) is the material of versification—interpretation by nomenclature effective in verse and prose; includes rhythm, mixture with the unfamiliar, and 'tune'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction should employ 'sweetened language' (rhythm, unfamiliar elements, tune) appropriately; language varies with character (e.g., child's speech plainer than a higher-class person). Diction is part of the clothing of the play but essential to poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music as a sweetening
rubrics_metrics.description: Music is 'the greatest of the sweetenings' and is 'a thing whose whole force is on the surface'—a direct appeal akin to a universal language; music's appeal is immediate and not deeply interpretive as verbal poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music should be varied to fit characters and moods; stage music may use imitative harmonies (hypodoristi, hypophrygisti) and at times can dominate metre. Use music to heighten surface effect while recognizing its different cognitive appeal from language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation / Exhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation (exhibition) is the staging, acting, and costume aspect; though fascinating, it is 'least amenable to scientific treatment' and 'least connected with Poetry' because it relies on particulars (locality, historical dress, actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet need not control all aspects of presentation—actors and costumiers affect actual success—so presentation is a supplementary factor. While physiognomy connects presentation to character, it remains less central to poetic craft than plot, character, and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and unity of action (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed story is a 'whole' with beginning, middle, and end: a Beginning follows nothing but leads to something by laws of nature or moral certainty; a Middle both follows and precedes; an End follows something and is followed by nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots must neither begin nor end at fortuitous points; beginnings and ends should be the points at which natural or morally certain causal chains start and cease. The story must embody these formulae to achieve unity and inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude/size and arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful story must have magnitude — enough length to be a whole but not more than the memory can retain; beauty requires proper size, arrangement, symmetry and limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a scope large enough to allow reversals (good fortune to bad or vice versa) yet limited so the audience can grasp the whole. Excessive length blurs unity; too small lacks sufficient substance. Practical suggestions include keeping performance duration within audience retention (historically suggested ~three hours but variable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity as single complete experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should portray one complete experience (a 'complete chapter of life') and the whole of it; the component parts must be arranged so that displacement or removal of any part would shatter the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to chronicle all events of a life; select the single experience that forms the coherent plot. The story's unity is not merely revolving around one person but presenting one integrated action or career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typicality and the province of the poet (potential, not merely the actual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's business is to treat the typical or the potential as regulated by moral certainty or laws of nature; poetry generalizes and formulates principles, whereas history particularizes facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventing or adapting stories, aim to represent what is generally true or logically follows from character traits and circumstances (the potentially necessary), rather than simply recording factual events. This is why poetry can be considered 'more scientific' as it explains causes rather than merely reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Believability / matter of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential in poetry must be believable: events that have occurred make their possibility credible; subjects too ancient or too recent may stretch belief—familiar names lend credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects and names to match audience expectations of plausibility. Use historical names when appropriate for credibility but do not obsessively adhere to tradition—fiction may invent while preserving the most important traditional features (e.g., Medea's deeds are more plausible under her name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot-driven emotional effect (tragedy requires events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic effect (drawing tears or horror) is produced by the action. Mere psychological orations, however exquisite, will fail to produce tragic effect if not embedded in incidents forming a coherent Story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize incidents that cause reversal, recognition, irony, or disclosure. Structure action so that emotions follow from events, not from isolated persuasive speeches or rhetorical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of all elements with character
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character has its own externals—story, diction, melody, and intellect—to correspond with character; looks, dress, music, and reasoning vary with character, age, and social class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor language, music, and presentation to the character: child's speech should be plainer; music and dress should reflect mood and status. Consistency between character traits and all other dramatic elements supports credibility and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of rhetorical training vs natural speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Older dramatists made characters speak naturally (like persons without rhetorical training), while modern dramatists often favor rhetorically trained speech; the former is preferable for natural character depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making all characters sound rhetorically trained unless the role requires it; naturalness in utterance helps convey character and maintain believability, reserving formal rhetorical speeches for characters whose role or status justifies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and diction as different cognitive appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Music 'has its whole force on the surface' with direct appeal and limited interpretability; verbal poetry admits of interpretation and varies with hearer's knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use music to provide immediate affective impact and diction for interpretive depth. Recognize that music functions differently from language in eliciting pleasure and should be integrated accordingly rather than treated as a substitute for poetic meaning.
